title: Number of Islands
statement:
An ad dashboard draws a heat map of a city as a grid. Each cell is '1' if ads in that area are active right now and '0' if not. The ops team wants to know how many separate clusters of active regions there are, so each one can get its own budget alert.

The grid is a list of strings of equal length; grid[r][c] is row r, column c. Two active cells belong to the same cluster when they touch up, down, left or right. Diagonal neighbours do not join clusters. Everything outside the grid counts as inactive.

Write def solution(grid) that returns the number of clusters as an integer. An empty grid ([]) has 0. Maps can hold 40,000 cells in one cluster, so use an explicit queue or stack, not recursion.

examples.why: The LeetCode 200 example 1. Every '1' is reachable from the top-left one by side steps.
The LeetCode 200 example 2: a 2 x 2 block, a single cell in the middle, and a pair at the bottom right.
The diagonal trap. Each '1' touches the others only at corners, so each is its own cluster.

constraints: every row has the same length
every character is '1' or '0' (strings, not integers)

think.a: A maximal group of '1' cells where you can walk from any cell to any other using only up, down, left and right steps on '1's. In graph terms: cells are nodes, side-touching land cells share an edge, and you are counting connected components.

think.q: Count ["110", "011", "001"] by hand. How did you avoid counting a cluster twice?
think.a: Scan row by row. At (0, 0) you find new land: count 1, then colour everything it reaches: (0, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 2). The rest of the scan only sees coloured cells, so the answer is 1. The trick is the colouring: once a cluster is marked, later cells of it are skipped.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: For every land cell, flood its whole cluster from scratch and count the cell only if it is the first cell of that cluster in reading order. Correct, but one big cluster of k cells is flooded k times: O((rows x cols)^2).

Scan plus flood fill (graph traversal on a grid). Scan every cell once; each unvisited land cell starts a new cluster, and a BFS with collections.deque (or a DFS with a list as a stack) marks the whole cluster visited. Every cell is enqueued at most once, so the total is O(rows x cols).

1. If the grid is empty, return 0.
  2. seen = a rows x cols grid of False.
  3. For each cell: if it is '1' and not seen, add 1 to the count, mark it, put it in a deque.
  4. While the deque is not empty: pop a cell, look at its 4 neighbours, and mark and enqueue each in-bounds, unseen '1'.
  5. Return the count.

Empty grid. One cell, land or water. All water (0) and all land (1). Diagonal-only contact (must stay separate). One row or one column (bounds checks on one axis). A ring with a separate cell inside it. A spiral that forces the fill to go up and left, not only down and right. A 40,000-cell cluster, which overflows Python's default recursion limit of 1,000 if you recurse.

hints: Treat the map as a graph: each land cell is a node, side-touching land cells are connected. You are counting connected components.
Scan every cell. When you find land you have not visited, that is a new cluster: count it, then visit every cell of it so the scan never counts it again.
Use deque([(r, c)]) and popleft(). Mark a cell as seen when you enqueue it, not when you pop it, or the same cell can enter the queue several times.
explain:
Example 2, ["11000", "11000", "00100", "00011"]:

  • (0, 0) is new land: count = 1. The BFS marks (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1) and stops, because every other neighbour is '0'.
  • The scan passes (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1): already seen, skipped.
  • (2, 2) is new land: count = 2. Its 4 neighbours are all water, so the BFS ends at once. (1, 1) and (3, 3) touch it only diagonally.
  • (3, 3) is new land: count = 3. The BFS adds (3, 4).

Return 3. Each cell is scanned once and enqueued at most once, so the work is O(rows x cols) however the clusters are shaped. The seen grid exists because Python strings are immutable; the other common answer copies the grid with [list(row) for row in grid] and 'sinks' land to '0' as it is visited.
complexity: O(rows x cols) time, O(rows x cols) extra space for the seen grid and the queue

talk: O(rows x cols) time: the outer scan touches each cell once and each land cell enters the deque at most once, because I mark it when I enqueue it.
I use collections.deque and popleft(), which is O(1); list.pop(0) is O(n) and turns a big cluster into quadratic work.
No recursion: a 200 x 200 all-land map is a 40,000-cell cluster and Python's default recursion limit is 1,000. An explicit deque or stack has no such limit.
Strings are immutable, so I keep a seen grid. If I am allowed to change the input, I copy it to a list of lists and overwrite visited land with '0', which saves the extra grid.
Neighbours as a tuple of four (nr, nc) pairs with one bounds check 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols keeps the edge handling in one place.
extensions: Return the size of the largest cluster (LC 695 Max Area of Island): count cells inside each BFS and keep the maximum.
Treat diagonal neighbours as touching too: which line changes, and what is example 3's answer then?
Regions switch on one at a time and you must report the cluster count after each one (LC 305): why is re-running the BFS too slow, and how does union-find fix it?
Count clusters with distinct shapes (LC 694): record each cluster's cells relative to its first cell and put that tuple in a set.
The map is too large for memory and arrives row by row: keep only the previous row's cluster labels and merge labels with union-find.
